overview.summary: Take your own business idea from a guess to its first paying customers, with free AI tools at every step and Indian examples from campus ventures to D2C (direct-to-consumer) brands. Seven practical modules cover evidence, a first version of your product, selling, marketing, networking, money and your team, and you finish with a two-week project with a mentor: an idea backed by real customer conversations. That is about 7 hours of modules, then about 8 hours of project work spread over two weeks. Legal set-up, such as registering a business and GST, is not covered in this version and will come in a later one.
overview.audience: students and recent graduates in India who want to start something of their own, from a campus venture to a small online business, and have never started one before
outcomes: Test a business idea through real customer conversations and judge how strong the evidence is
Build a no-code first version of a product and test it with five users against a goal set in advance
Win first customers by selling in messages, collecting payment by UPI, and growing through marketing, your network and referrals
Price an offer and plan unit economics, cash flow and first funding in rupees
Plan a founding team: one owner for each area and, if you have co-founders, a written equity split with vesting
Use free AI tools to research, draft and practise, and check everything they produce

items.statement: Before I decide a problem is real, I ask people how they deal with it today.
When an AI chatbot gives me a fact or a number, I check it against a source I can open.
When friends say my idea is great, I take it as a sign that the idea will work.
When I try something new, I start with a small, rough version to see if it works.
Before I try something out, I decide what result would count as a success.
I prefer to finish a piece of work completely before I show it to anyone.
When I offer something to someone, I end by asking them for a clear decision.
When someone raises a doubt about my offer, I ask what is behind it before I reply.
When someone doesn’t reply to my first message, I don’t contact them again.
Before I post or share something, I think about exactly who it is for.
I judge whether a post worked by what people did afterwards, not only by its likes.
I post the same thing in as many places as I can, so that more people see it.
I contact people a step or two ahead of me, such as seniors or alumni, to ask for advice.
When I ask someone for help, I say exactly what I need and how much time it will take.
I wait for useful people to come to me, rather than reaching out to them first.
I keep track of the money I spend and receive each week or month.
Before I agree a price for something I sell or organise, I work out what it costs me.
I find out how much money I have left only when it starts to run low.
When I work in a group, I make sure each task has one named person responsible for it.
Before a group project starts, I agree with the others how much time each of us can give.
When I work with friends, I leave who does what unspoken, because we know each other well.

modules.title: Evaluate an idea with evidence
modules.summary: Turn an idea into a clear problem and customer group, ask questions about real behaviour, and judge how strong your evidence is.
modules.outcome: Write an interview script that tests your idea’s problem with a named customer group, using only questions about past behaviour.

learn.title: Start with a problem and a customer, not a product
learn.body:
Most first ideas are solutions, like “a laundry app for students”. Customers don’t buy apps. They pay to make a problem go away. So write your idea as one sentence: who has the problem, what it is, and how they cope today.

Worked example: Ananya in Pune wants to start a laundry pickup service. Her first version was “a laundry app for students”. Her sharper version: “First-year hostel students at three Pune colleges lose two hours every Sunday washing clothes by hand, because the nearest laundry is 3 km away.”

Now she knows whom to talk to and what to ask about. Notice the customer group, called a segment. It is a specific group, not “all students”. Here is a useful test. If people in your group describe the problem in completely different ways, the group is too broad. Make it smaller.

learn.title: Ask about the past, not about your idea
learn.body:
People are polite. Ask “Would you use my laundry service?” and most will say yes. That tells you nothing. The book The Mom Test by Rob Fitzpatrick gives a simple rule: ask what people actually did, not what they think of your idea.

Compare these two questions.
Weak: “Would you pay ₹200 a week for laundry pickup?”
Strong: “Tell me about the last time you did your laundry. How long did it take? What did it cost? What have you tried to make it easier?”

The strong questions show real behaviour. Maybe someone already pays a dhobi, bought a bucket washer, or walks 3 km every week. Then the problem is real for them.

Talk less than half the time, and don’t describe your idea until the end. Common mistake: counting compliments like “Great idea!” as evidence. A compliment costs the speaker nothing.

learn.title: Weigh your evidence: from compliments to commitments
learn.body:
Not all evidence is equal. Picture a ladder, from weakest to strongest:
1. Compliments and promises (“Nice idea”, “I would buy it”).
2. Past spending of time or money on the problem.
3. A commitment of time (a second meeting, trying a free trial) or of reputation (introducing you to friends).
4. A commitment of money (a pre-order or a deposit).

Worked example: Ananya spoke to 8 students. Six said it was a great idea (rung 1). Four already paid a dhobi about ₹150 a week (rung 2). Two booked a free trial pickup (rung 3). One paid a ₹100 deposit by UPI (rung 4). Her case rests on the top three rungs, not the six compliments.

Good habits: ask before you record a conversation. Remove names and phone numbers before you paste notes into any AI tool.

learn.title: AI can prepare you, but only people are evidence
learn.body:
A free AI chatbot (the free versions of ChatGPT, Gemini or Claude) is a fast research helper. It can draft interview questions, suggest who to talk to, and list ways people solve a problem today.

It can also pretend to be “a typical student” and answer your questions. Those answers sound real, but they are not evidence. In 2024 tests by the research firm Nielsen Norman Group, AI “synthetic users” praised almost every idea, while real users raised doubts.

Worked example: Ananya asked a chatbot to act as a hostel student. It said it would “definitely” pay ₹200 a week. Two of the real students she met said ₹150 was already too much. Only the real answers counted.

Use AI to prepare for conversations and to sort your notes afterwards. Never use it in place of the conversations.

learn.title: Size the market from the bottom up
learn.body:
AI also invents numbers. Ask it about “India’s laundry market” and you may get a big crore figure with no real source. Use an AI figure only if you can open its source and check it.

Instead, size your market from the bottom up, from numbers you can check yourself.

Worked example: Ananya asked the hostel offices how many first-year students live in. The answer was about 1,200 in each of three colleges.
3 colleges × 1,200 students = 3,600 students.
Her guess: 1 in 10 would pay ₹600 a month. That is what students already pay a dhobi (₹150 a week). 360 students × ₹600 = ₹2.16 lakh a month.
The “1 in 10” is a guess, and two students called ₹150 a week too much. She marked both to test in interviews.

Finally, list the substitutes: the dhobi, a washing machine in a PG (paying-guest housing), washing by hand. Common mistake: saying “we have no competitors”. There is always some alternative.

tasks.title: Fix weak interview questions
tasks.prompt:
Kabir in Bhopal plans a ₹99-a-month app that shares class notes with engineering students. These are his interview questions:
1. Would you use an app that has all your notes?
2. How much would you pay for it?
3. Don’t you hate searching for notes before exams?
4. Would you recommend it to your friends?
5. What features do you want?
Rewrite each one as a question about past behaviour. Then write two lines on what answer would count as strong evidence, and on which rung of the ladder it would sit.
tasks.hint: Start your questions with “Tell me about the last time…”, “What did you do when…” or “What have you tried…”. A strong answer names a real event, a cost in time or money, or something the person already tried.

tasks.title: Your idea: problem, script and size
tasks.prompt:
Use your own idea, or this one: a home-cooked tiffin service for PG residents in Hyderabad.
1. Write a one-sentence problem statement: who, what problem, and how they cope today.
2. Ask a free AI chatbot to draft 8 interview questions for that group. Rewrite or delete every question that asks for an opinion or a promise about the future.
3. Make a bottom-up estimate: reachable customers × share who might pay × price × times a month. Write where each number came from, and mark any number you could not check.
4. List three substitutes your customers use today.
tasks.hint: Give the AI the rule in your prompt: “Ask only about past behaviour. Don’t mention my idea.” Then check its work anyway, because it often slips in “Would you…” questions. A number you counted yourself, like rooms in a PG, beats a big figure from AI.

reflection.prompt: Which part of your idea are you most sure about? What evidence do you actually have for it, and which rung of the ladder is it on?
reflection.hint: If your answer is “my friends said it’s a good idea”, that is the bottom rung. Name two people you could ask about their past behaviour this week.

quiz.title: Courts in Indore
quiz.scenario: Nikhil in Indore wants to build an app that shows free badminton courts near colleges. He is writing his first interview questions for students who play twice a week.
quiz.question: Which question will give him the most useful evidence?
options: Would you use an app that shows which courts near your college are free?
How much would you pay each month for an app that books courts for you?
Don’t you find it annoying when every court near your college is already full?
Tell me about the last time you wanted to play. How did you find a court?
quiz.explanation: It asks about a real, recent event, so the answer shows what students actually do today and what it costs them. That is evidence about the problem, not an opinion about Nikhil’s idea.
quiz.why_wrong: “Would you use…” asks for a promise about the future, and polite people say yes. “How much would you pay…” asks for a guess about a price for something they haven’t seen. “Don’t you find it annoying…” leads the person to agree, so the answer tells him nothing new.
quiz.learning_outcome: Ask about past behaviour, not opinions of your idea.

quiz.title: Four interview notes
quiz.scenario: Lakshmi in Madurai plans a weekend coding club for Class 8 students. She has notes from four interviews with parents.
quiz.question: Which note sits highest on the evidence ladder?
options: Mrs Iyer introduced her to her son’s school parents’ group and set up a meeting.
Mrs Rao said she would definitely enrol her son on the day the club first opens.
Mr Khan bought his son a ₹400 coding workbook from a bookshop last term.
Mr Das said it was the best idea for children that he had heard all year.
quiz.explanation: Mrs Iyer put her own reputation behind Lakshmi by introducing her to other parents, and gave her time to set up a meeting. That is a commitment, the third rung of the ladder. Mr Khan’s workbook is past spending on the problem, the second rung: useful, but he has committed nothing to Lakshmi.
quiz.why_wrong: Mrs Rao’s “definitely” is a promise about the future, the bottom rung, however sure it sounds. Mr Khan’s workbook shows he has spent money on coding before, which is the second rung, below a commitment to Lakshmi herself. Mr Das’s praise is a compliment, the bottom rung, because it costs him nothing.
quiz.learning_outcome: Rank evidence on the ladder: compliments, past spending, commitments, money.

quiz.title: Tiffins in Madhapur
quiz.scenario: Sameer is sizing a tiffin service for PG residents in Madhapur, Hyderabad. He counted 40 PGs on a walk, and the owners said each has about 25 residents. Six residents he interviewed pay ₹2,400 a month for tiffins now. He assumes that 1 in 5 residents would switch to him.
quiz.question: Which number in his estimate most needs testing in his next interviews?
options: The 1 in 5 who would switch, because it is only his own guess
The 40 PGs, because he counted them himself on a single walk
The 25 residents a PG, because the owners gave him that figure
The ₹2,400 price, because only six residents told him what they pay
quiz.explanation: Every other number comes from something Sameer counted or was told by people who know. The share who would switch is his own guess, and it changes the answer most: 40 × 25 = 1,000 residents, and 1 in 5 of them at ₹2,400 is ₹4.8 lakh a month. He should mark it as a guess and test it.
quiz.why_wrong: The 40 PGs are a count he made himself, the strongest kind of number. The 25 residents come from the owners, who know their own buildings. The ₹2,400 is what real residents already pay, which is past behaviour, even if more answers would help.
quiz.learning_outcome: In a bottom-up estimate, find and test the number that is only a guess.

quiz.title: Twenty AI students
quiz.scenario: Aditi wants to sell second-hand lab coats to first-year students in Nagpur. She asked a free AI chatbot to act as 20 different first-year students. 18 of them said they would buy a coat for ₹250.
quiz.question: What should she do with these answers?
options: Use them to plan questions, then ask real students how they got a coat
Report to her mentor that about 90% of first-years would buy a coat
Ask the chatbot to act as 200 students, so that the sample is bigger
Count them as evidence, but halve the figure to allow for the AI’s bias
quiz.explanation: AI “synthetic users” sound real, but they are not evidence: in tests they praised almost every idea while real users raised doubts. Their answers can suggest what to ask. Only real first-years’ past behaviour, such as how they got a coat last term, counts.
quiz.why_wrong: Reporting 90% presents AI guesses as customer evidence. A bigger AI sample repeats the same bias 200 times. Halving the figure still treats an invented number as data.
quiz.learning_outcome: Use AI to prepare for interviews, never in place of real people.

modules.title: Build and test a scrappy MVP
modules.summary: Find your riskiest assumption, test it with the cheapest version of your product, and learn from five real users.
modules.outcome: Build a no-code MVP that tests your riskiest assumption, with a five-user test plan and a success goal set in advance.

learn.title: An MVP tests your riskiest assumption
learn.body:
An MVP (minimum viable product) is the smallest thing that shows whether your idea works with real people. It is not a cheap copy of the full app. It is a test.

Start by listing your assumptions: the things that must be true for the business to work. Then pick the riskiest one. That is the one that would end the idea if it were wrong.

Worked example: Joel in Kochi wants to deliver home-baked birthday cakes to college hostels. His assumptions: students order cakes for friends’ birthdays; they will pay ₹450 for a 500 g cake in advance; he can deliver within two hours. He already knows students buy cakes. The riskiest assumption is paying ₹450 in advance. So his MVP is one Instagram post, orders on WhatsApp and a UPI advance, for one week. No app.

Common mistake: spending three months building an app before anyone has paid.

learn.title: Four scrappy MVPs you can build on a phone
learn.body:
You can test most ideas with free tools and no code.

1. Concierge: you deliver the service by hand to a few customers. Ananya from Module 1 could collect laundry herself with a bag and a bike.
2. A one-page offer: a Google Form or a simple web page that describes the offer, the price and how to order. Count how many people fill it in.
3. A WhatsApp Business catalogue: list each product with a photo and a price, then take orders in chat. The WhatsApp Business app is free.
4. Wizard of Oz: it looks automatic, but you do the work behind the scenes. For example, a “personalised study plan” that you write yourself for each student.

Choose the type that tests your riskiest assumption fastest. Joel’s question was “Will they pay in advance?”, so he needed a real price and a real payment, not just likes.

learn.title: Use AI to build faster, then check it
learn.body:
AI app builders, such as Lovable, Bolt and v0, turn a written description into a web page or a simple app. Their free plans limit how much you can build each day, and those limits change often. Check the current limits before you start.

You may not need a builder at all. A free AI chatbot can write the words for your Google Form or catalogue.

Worked example: Joel typed, “Write a one-screen offer for home-baked birthday cakes delivered to Kochi college hostels. Include a headline, three short points, the price of ₹450 for 500 g, and an order button that opens WhatsApp.” The draft said “Loved by 500+ students”. That was false, so he deleted it.

Before you share an AI draft, check four things. Is every claim true? Is the price right? Does it open properly on a phone? Are AI-made images labelled, so nobody thinks they show your real product?

learn.title: Test with five users and decide in advance
learn.body:
Before you test, write your success goal: a number, a group and a time. For example: “At least 3 of 5 hostel students pre-order with a ₹100 advance within 48 hours.” Writing it first stops you from calling any result a success afterwards.

During the test, give the person your MVP and watch. Don’t help or explain. Ask them to say what they are thinking. Note every place they stop, frown or ask a question.

Worked example: Joel showed his offer to 5 students. Two ordered. Three got stuck because the post did not say when the cake would arrive. He had missed his goal, but the reason was clear and easy to fix.

After a test, make one of three decisions. Keep going, if you met the goal. Change one thing and test again, if the reason is clear. Stop or rethink, if nobody cares about the problem.

tasks.title: Choose the riskiest assumption and the MVP
tasks.prompt:
Meghna in Guwahati wants to sell handmade bamboo desk organisers to college students for ₹349 each, through Instagram.
1. List five assumptions that must be true for her business to work.
2. Rank them from riskiest to safest, with one line of reason for the top one.
3. Choose one of the four MVP types to test the riskiest assumption, and describe it in three lines.
4. Write her success goal: a number, a group and a time.
tasks.hint: Ask yourself which assumption, if wrong, would end the business. “Students like bamboo” is easy to check. “Students will pay ₹349 for a desk organiser” is harder, and more important.

tasks.title: Build a one-screen MVP for your idea
tasks.prompt:
Build a first MVP for your own idea, or for Meghna’s. Use a free tool: a Google Form, a WhatsApp Business catalogue item, or one page in an AI builder’s free plan. It must say who it is for, the problem, the offer, the price and how to order.
Use a free AI chatbot to draft the words. Then mark every change you made to keep it true.
Finally, write a five-user test plan: your success goal, the three things you will watch for, and the one question you will ask at the end. Open it on your phone to check it works.
tasks.hint: Keep it to one screen. If you catch yourself adding a login, a menu or a second page, stop. You are testing one assumption, not building the whole product.

reflection.prompt: What were you planning to build before this module? What is the smallest test that would tell you whether to build it at all?
reflection.hint: A good MVP feels a little embarrassing. If it took more than a day to make, look for something smaller.

quiz.title: Lunch boxes in Indore
quiz.scenario: Tara in Indore wants to sell weekly lunch boxes to office workers near Vijay Nagar, at ₹1,100 a week paid in advance. She has seen long queues at the lunch stalls there. She has cooked for 40 guests at family functions. She has not yet asked anyone to pay a week ahead.
quiz.question: Which assumption is riskiest, so that her MVP should test it first?
options: Office workers near Vijay Nagar need to buy lunch on working days
Tara can cook enough good lunches for a whole group every day
Office workers will pay ₹1,100 before the week has even started
Her lunch boxes will look attractive in photos on Instagram
quiz.explanation: If nobody pays a week ahead, the business fails, and Tara has no evidence on it yet. The queues already show that people buy lunch there, and the family functions show she can cook in quantity, so those assumptions are safer.
quiz.why_wrong: The need for lunch is already shown by the queues. Cooking for 40 guests is some evidence she can cope, and she can check it during a small test. How the boxes look in photos matters for marketing, but being wrong about it would not end the business.
quiz.learning_outcome: Test first the assumption that would end the idea if it were wrong.

quiz.title: Placement plans
quiz.scenario: Rohit in Pune wants to sell personalised placement-preparation plans to final-year students for ₹299. He imagines an app that uses AI to write each plan. His riskiest assumption is that students will pay ₹299 for a personal plan.
quiz.question: Which MVP tests that assumption fastest?
options: Build the app in an AI builder’s free plan, then invite students to try it
An Instagram poll asking final-year students whether they want a personal plan
A one-page site where students can join a free waiting list for the app’s launch
A Google Form that takes orders and ₹299 by UPI, with plans he writes himself
quiz.explanation: This is a Wizard of Oz MVP: the student gets a finished plan, Rohit does the work by hand, and a real ₹299 payment answers his riskiest question. He can set it up in an hour with free tools.
quiz.why_wrong: Building the app first takes far longer and still doesn’t ask anyone to pay. A poll collects opinions, which cost nothing to give. A free waiting list shows interest, not willingness to pay ₹299.
quiz.learning_outcome: Choose the MVP that tests the riskiest assumption with a real action.

quiz.title: The order form test
quiz.scenario: Before her test, Neha wrote: “At least 3 of 5 hostel students order a ₹200 snack box through my Google Form within 48 hours.” One student ordered. Three others said they wanted a box, but the form asked for payment before it showed the delivery day, so they stopped.
quiz.question: What should Neha decide?
options: Call it a success, since 4 of the 5 students wanted to order a box
Stop the idea, since only 1 of the 5 students actually ordered a box
Spend a month building an app, since the Google Form is the problem
Show the delivery day before the payment step, then test again
quiz.explanation: She missed the goal she set in advance, so it is not a success. But the reason is clear and easy to fix, so the right decision is to change that one thing and run the test again.
quiz.why_wrong: Counting “wanted to” as success moves the goal after the result, and wanting is not ordering. Stopping ignores that three people tried to order and were blocked by the form, not by the idea. Building an app is a big, slow fix for a problem that one change to the form can solve.
quiz.learning_outcome: Judge a test against the goal set in advance, then keep, change or stop.

quiz.title: Watching a user
quiz.scenario: Vikram is testing his one-page offer for a cycle-repair pickup service with a student in Mysuru. The student scrolls, stops at the price, frowns and goes quiet.
quiz.question: What should Vikram do at that moment?
options: Explain the price clearly, so that the student can finish the test
Move on, and ask at the end whether the student liked the page
Offer a lower price straight away, so that the student doesn’t leave
Note where the student stopped, and ask what they are thinking
quiz.explanation: The stop and the frown are exactly what the test is for. Noting them and asking the student to say what they are thinking, without explaining, shows what a real customer would get stuck on.
quiz.why_wrong: Explaining helps this student, but real customers won’t have Vikram beside them, so it hides the problem. Asking “did you like it?” at the end invites a polite compliment. Cutting the price guesses at the problem before he knows what it is.
quiz.learning_outcome: In a user test, watch and ask; don’t help or explain.

modules.title: Sell to your first customers
modules.summary: Find your first buyers among people you can reach, pitch in a minute, handle doubts, and turn a yes into a UPI payment.
modules.outcome: Write a one-minute pitch that ends with a clear ask for a UPI payment or pre-order, with replies to common doubts and a follow-up message.

learn.title: Start with a warm list
learn.body:
Your first customers rarely come from ads. They come from a warm list: people who already know you, or who share a place with you. Think of classmates, your hostel wing, your family’s circle, and the people you interviewed in Module 1.

Worked example: Fatima in Lucknow sells tote bags with chikankari embroidery for ₹599. She wrote down 30 names. Then she marked the 12 who had told her they bought gifts recently. Those 12 became her first messages.

Write to each person, not to a group. A broadcast like “Please buy my bags!” sent to every contact feels like spam. Fatima’s message was personal: “Riya, you said you struggle to find gifts under ₹1,000. I’ve started making these. Can I send you photos?”

A free AI chatbot can draft a message for each type of person. Always edit the draft so it sounds like you.

learn.title: A one-minute pitch that ends with an ask
learn.body:
A pitch is a short explanation of your offer. Keep it to about a minute, in five parts:
1. The problem, in the customer’s own words.
2. What you offer.
3. Proof: what early users did or said.
4. The price.
5. The ask: one clear next step.

Worked example: “You told me finding a gift under ₹1,000 is hard. I make hand-embroidered chikankari totes. Each takes about six hours. My first five buyers gave them as birthday gifts, and two came back for a second one. They cost ₹599. Shall I keep one for you for Saturday? You can pay a ₹200 advance by UPI.”

Common mistake: ending with “Let me know if you’re interested.” That asks for no decision, so you usually get none. Ask for something specific.

learn.title: Handle doubts by asking, not arguing
learn.body:
When someone says “too expensive” or “I’ll think about it”, they are giving you information. Don’t argue. Use three steps: listen, ask a question to understand, then answer with a fact or a smaller step.

Worked example:
Customer: “₹599 is too much.”
Fatima: “What would you compare it with?”
Customer: “A mall tote costs ₹400.”
Fatima: “That’s fair. The difference is six hours of hand embroidery. I also make a smaller pouch for ₹349.”

Common doubts are about price, timing (“not now”) and trust (“will it really arrive?”). For trust, offer proof: photos of real orders, a delivery date, a clear refund promise.

You can practise with AI. Ask a chatbot to play a doubtful customer for your product. This is practice only. As Module 1 showed, an AI’s answers are not evidence about real customers.

learn.title: Turn a yes into a payment, then follow up
learn.body:
A yes becomes real when money moves. Ask for payment or an advance by UPI. Show your UPI QR code, or send your UPI ID or a payment link. Since October 2025, one person can’t send another a UPI payment request, so you can’t “request” the money.

A pre-order is strong proof, even before you have stock. Give a delivery date and a clear refund promise. If you can’t deliver, refund at once.

Instagram removed its Shop tab in 2023. Most small Indian sellers now show products in posts and sell in direct messages and WhatsApp, then collect by UPI.

For follow-up, the WhatsApp Business app is free. It has a catalogue, quick replies (saved answers to common questions) and labels such as “New”, “Paid” and “Delivered”. Follow up within a day, once or twice, then stop.

Worked example: Fatima labels chats “Paid” only after the UPI money shows in her bank app. A screenshot can be faked.

tasks.title: Write the pitch and handle two doubts
tasks.prompt:
Karthik in Coimbatore runs weekend spoken-English classes for Class 10 students, at ₹1,500 a month. In his interviews, four parents said their children freeze when they speak English in class.
1. Write his one-minute pitch to a parent (about 120 words), using the five parts. End with a specific ask that includes a UPI advance.
2. Write his replies to two doubts: “It’s too expensive” and “Let me ask my husband first.” Use the three steps: listen, ask, answer.
tasks.hint: Use the parents’ own words for the problem. For “let me ask my husband”, offer something that helps that conversation, such as a free trial class both parents can watch.

tasks.title: Build your sales kit
tasks.prompt:
For your own idea, or for Karthik’s classes, prepare:
1. A warm list of 15 people (initials only), with one line each on why they might buy.
2. Three quick replies of under 50 words each: the price, how to pay by UPI, and when it will be delivered or start.
3. One follow-up message for a person who said “maybe” yesterday.
Use a free AI chatbot to draft the replies, then rewrite them in your own voice. If you can, save them as quick replies in the free WhatsApp Business app. If not, keep them in your phone’s notes app.
tasks.hint: A good quick reply answers the question and suggests the next step. “₹1,500 a month, 8 classes. Want to try the first one free this Saturday?” works better than a price alone.

reflection.prompt: What makes you uncomfortable about asking people for money? What would make your ask feel fair to you and to them?
reflection.hint: Most first-time founders feel this. An ask feels fair when it solves a problem the person told you about, at a clear price, with an honest refund promise.

quiz.title: Ending the pitch
quiz.scenario: Sunita in Nashik makes ₹450 birthday hampers that college students send to friends in other cities. She is pitching to a student in her college. She has described the problem, the hamper, what early buyers did and the price.
quiz.question: Which last line is the best way to end her pitch?
options: “Let me know if you want one, and I can send you more photos later.”
“Shall I keep one for you to send on Friday? A ₹150 UPI advance holds it.”
“Do you think other students in your hostel would like a hamper like this?”
“I’d be really grateful for your support for my small new business.”
quiz.explanation: It asks for one clear decision with a specific next step: one hamper, sent on a named day, held by a small UPI advance. A clear ask gets a clear yes or no, and either answer tells Sunita something.
quiz.why_wrong: “Let me know” asks for no decision, so usually none comes. Asking about other students changes the subject from this student’s own choice. Asking for support turns a sale into a favour, and favours rarely turn into paying customers.
quiz.learning_outcome: End a pitch with one clear, specific ask.

quiz.title: Too expensive
quiz.scenario: Deepa in Kolkata sells hand-painted phone covers for ₹449. A college student she is talking to says, “₹449 is too much for a phone cover.”
quiz.question: What is the best next reply?
options: “It’s actually cheap for hand-painted work.”
“For you, I can make it ₹300 instead.”
“What would you compare it with?”
“Only two are left, so decide soon.”
quiz.explanation: The doubt is information. Asking what the student compares it with shows the real objection, for example a ₹200 cover from a market stall. Deepa can then answer with a fact about her work or offer a smaller option.
quiz.why_wrong: Calling it cheap argues instead of listening, so the student defends her view. A discount at once teaches buyers that the price isn’t real and cuts Deepa’s margin before she knows the reason. “Only two left” pressures instead of answering, and it is false urgency unless it is true.
quiz.learning_outcome: Handle a doubt by listening and asking before answering.

quiz.title: Wedding videos
quiz.scenario: Harpreet in Amritsar has started making personalised wedding invitation videos for ₹2,000. She has 300 phone contacts. In her interviews, 9 people told her a family wedding is coming up in the next three months.
quiz.question: How should she look for her first customers?
options: Send one broadcast message about the videos to all 300 of her contacts
Write to each of the 9 people, mentioning the wedding they told her about
Post about the videos in every family and college WhatsApp group she is in
Boost an Instagram post to people in Punjab who are interested in weddings
quiz.explanation: The 9 people are her warmest list: they know her and have a real, dated need. A personal message that mentions their wedding is relevant to each of them, and she can follow up one by one.
quiz.why_wrong: A broadcast to all 300 feels like spam, and most of them have no wedding coming. Posting in every group reaches people with no need and can annoy the members. A paid boost spends money on strangers before she has sold to the people who already need her service.
quiz.learning_outcome: Start selling with a warm list and personal messages.

quiz.title: The late delivery
quiz.scenario: Raghav took 8 pre-orders for custom cricket-bat grips at ₹350, each with a ₹150 UPI advance and a promise of delivery on Saturday. On Thursday, his supplier says that 3 of the grips will be a week late.
quiz.question: What should Raghav do?
options: Say nothing yet, and deliver those 3 grips next Saturday instead
Offer the 3 buyers ₹50 off a future order instead of any refund
Deliver to those 3 first, and make the other 5 buyers wait a week
Tell the 3 buyers today, and refund at once anyone who won’t wait
quiz.explanation: A pre-order is a promise. Telling the buyers early, and returning the advance at once to anyone who doesn’t want to wait, keeps their trust. That trust brings repeat orders and referrals.
quiz.why_wrong: Saying nothing breaks the promise without warning, and the buyers find out on Saturday. A discount on a future order keeps their money for a product they haven’t received. Moving the delay onto the other 5 buyers breaks five promises to keep three.
quiz.learning_outcome: Keep pre-order promises honest: tell buyers early and refund at once.

modules.title: Market on a tiny budget
modules.summary: Say clearly who you are for, pick one channel, make honest content with AI, and test ₹1,000 of spending against one measure.
modules.outcome: Plan a ₹1,000 marketing test on one channel, with honest AI-assisted content and one measure that decides what you do next.

learn.title: Positioning: one customer, one promise
learn.body:
Positioning is the short answer to “Who is this for, and why choose it?” Without it, every post you make says something different.

Use this template:
For [customer group] who [problem], [product] is a [type of product] that [main benefit]. Unlike [the alternative], it [what is different].

Worked example: Simran in Ludhiana makes protein laddoos. Her first line was “Healthy, tasty snacks for everyone”. That could describe a thousand brands. Her positioning: “For college students who go to the gym and skip breakfast, Simran’s Laddoos are a homemade protein snack that fits in a pocket. Unlike gym protein bars, they use no added sugar and cost ₹30 each.”

Now she knows whom to talk to, what to show and what to say. Common mistake: trying to appeal to everyone. A clear “for these people” attracts the right ones.

learn.title: Pick one channel where your customers already are
learn.body:
A channel is the way customers hear about you. Examples include Instagram posts and Reels, WhatsApp status, community WhatsApp groups (with the admin’s permission), college notice boards and events, YouTube Shorts and partner shops.

Choose one channel first, using three questions. Where does your customer group already spend time? Your interviews will tell you. What does it cost? What can you do well and keep doing every week?

Worked example: Simran planned to post on Instagram, YouTube and Facebook. But in her interviews, 7 of 10 gym-goers said they found deals through their gym’s WhatsApp group and the notice board. So she started there, with free posts and free samples. Instagram could wait.

Common mistake: posting a little on five platforms. You learn nothing, because no channel gets enough effort to show a result.

learn.title: Make content with AI, then make it true
learn.body:
A free AI chatbot can draft captions, opening lines for Reels and short scripts. Free design tools, such as Canva’s free plan, help with images. The danger is that AI writes confident claims that are not true.

Worked example: Simran asked for an Instagram caption. The draft said “Doctor-recommended, 20 g protein, only 3 left!” None of it was true. Her laddoos have about 6 g of protein, by her own recipe calculation. No doctor had seen them. She had 40 in stock. Her edited caption: “6 g protein, no added sugar, made fresh in Ludhiana every Monday. ₹30 each.”

Check every draft against three rules. Every claim must be true and checkable. There must be no false urgency, such as “only 3 left” when there are 40. The price must be the full price, with no extra charges added at payment. And if an image is AI-made, label it.

learn.title: Run a ₹1,000 test with one measure
learn.body:
A small test with a clear measure teaches you more than a big spend. Before you start, write down: what you believe, the channel, how much you will spend, the one measure, and what you will do with each result.

Worked example: Simran split ₹1,000 into two parts. She spent ₹600 on 30 sample laddoos at two gyms, and ₹400 to boost an Instagram post for four days. Her measure was orders, not likes. Each offer had its own code word, so she knew where an order came from. Gym orders said “GYM”. Instagram orders said “INSTA”.
Result: 9 GYM orders, cost per order ₹600 ÷ 9 = about ₹67.
2 INSTA orders, cost per order ₹400 ÷ 2 = ₹200.
She chose the gyms.

One small test is a hint, not proof. Meta does not publish a fixed minimum budget for ads, but small budgets give noisy results. Common mistake: judging by views and likes instead of orders.

tasks.title: Position an offer and choose its channel
tasks.prompt:
Imran in Hyderabad buys used engineering textbooks from final-year students and sells them to first-years at half the shop price. In his interviews, most first-years said they find books through seniors and their class WhatsApp group.
1. Write his positioning statement using the template.
2. Choose his one channel, with two reasons from the facts given.
3. Name two channels he should not start with, and say why.
tasks.hint: Base the channel on what the interviews say, not on what is popular. Think about when first-years most need books, and where they are at that moment.

tasks.title: Plan your ₹1,000 test and make one post
tasks.prompt:
For your own idea, or for Imran’s books:
1. Write a test plan with six lines: what you believe, the channel, how you split the ₹1,000, the one measure, how you will track where results came from, and what you will do if the result is good or bad.
2. Ask a free AI chatbot for one post or caption for that channel. Write the draft down, then rewrite it.
3. List each change you made and why: a false claim, false urgency, a hidden charge or an unlabelled AI image.
tasks.hint: Your measure should be something that costs the customer effort, such as orders, sign-ups or replies, not views. A code word, a separate WhatsApp number or a separate form link shows where each result came from. No budget? Plan a ₹0 test instead: free posts in one group and samples you make yourself, measured the same way.

reflection.prompt: Think of a small brand you bought from because of a post or a recommendation. What exactly made you trust it enough to pay?
reflection.hint: Often it is something specific and true: a real photo, a friend’s word, a clear price. Use the same in your own marketing.

quiz.title: Millet cookies
quiz.scenario: Anjali in Pune sells millet cookies. Her interviews found that most buyers are working mothers who want a snack with no maida for their children’s school tiffin.
quiz.question: Which positioning statement is strongest?
options: For everyone who loves healthy food, Anjali’s Cookies are a tasty, fresh and fairly priced snack.
For mothers packing school tiffins, Anjali’s millet cookies are a no-maida snack, unlike biscuits.
Anjali’s Cookies give you the best quality, the best taste and the best price of any brand in Pune.
Anjali’s Cookies come in eight flavours, made for children, adults, gym-goers and senior citizens.
quiz.explanation: It names one customer group and their need, the main benefit, and what makes it different from the usual alternative. Every post can now speak to those mothers.
quiz.why_wrong: “Everyone who loves healthy food” could describe a thousand brands and names no problem. “Best quality, taste and price” is a claim every seller makes and nobody can check. Eight flavours for every age group tries to appeal to everyone, so it speaks to no one.
quiz.learning_outcome: Position for one customer with one clear promise.

quiz.title: A stall or a boost
quiz.scenario: Manish in Jaipur ran a ₹1,000 test for his hand-block-printed cushion covers. He spent ₹500 on a stall at a college fest and got 10 orders. He spent ₹500 boosting an Instagram post and got 6,000 views, 140 likes and 4 orders. Each offer had its own code word.
quiz.question: What should he conclude from the test?
options: Instagram did better, because it reached 6,000 people for the same ₹500
Instagram did better, because 140 likes show more interest in the covers
The stall did better, at ₹50 an order against ₹125 an order on Instagram
Neither did better, because both channels brought him at least some orders
quiz.explanation: His measure is orders, and the code words show where each order came from. ₹500 ÷ 10 = ₹50 an order at the stall; ₹500 ÷ 4 = ₹125 on Instagram. One small test is a hint, not proof, so he should try the stall again and keep measuring.
quiz.why_wrong: Views cost the viewer nothing, so 6,000 of them don’t show that anyone will pay. Likes show interest, not orders. Both channels brought orders, but at very different costs, and finding that difference is what the test was for.
quiz.learning_outcome: Judge a marketing test by cost per order, not by views or likes.

quiz.title: The soap caption
quiz.scenario: Pooja in Surat sells handmade neem and aloe soaps for ₹120 each, plus ₹30 for packing. She has 50 in stock, and no doctor has tested them. A free AI chatbot wrote the caption “Dermatologist-approved! Only 3 left! ₹120.”
quiz.question: Which caption should she post?
options: “Loved by skin experts! Only 3 left! ₹120, plus ₹30 packing at checkout.”
“Handmade in Surat with neem and aloe. ₹150 a soap, packing included.”
“Dermatologist-approved and handmade in Surat with neem and aloe. ₹120.”
“Handmade in Surat with neem and aloe. Only 3 left! ₹120 + small charge.”
quiz.explanation: Every claim in it is true, there is no false urgency, and the price shown is the full price the buyer pays. Showing ₹150 up front is honest; adding a charge only at checkout hides part of the price.
quiz.why_wrong: “Loved by skin experts” is the same false claim in softer words, and “only 3 left” is false with 50 in stock. “Dermatologist-approved” repeats a claim no doctor made, and ₹120 hides the ₹30 added later. “Small charge” still hides part of the price, and the urgency is false.
quiz.learning_outcome: Check AI content for false claims, false urgency and hidden charges.

quiz.title: Where pickle buyers look
quiz.scenario: Shalini in Bengaluru makes home-made pickles. In her interviews, 8 of 10 buyers in her apartment complex said they find home food sellers through the residents’ WhatsApp group. She plans to post on Instagram, YouTube and Facebook every week.
quiz.question: Where should she start?
options: On all three platforms, a little on each, to reach the most people
On Instagram Reels, since short videos are popular with everyone
On YouTube Shorts, since it is free and her videos will last longer
In the residents’ WhatsApp group, with the group admin’s permission
quiz.explanation: Her interviews show where her customers already look for sellers like her. One channel, used well and with the admin’s permission, will show a result quickly. The other platforms can wait until this one works.
quiz.why_wrong: A little on three platforms spreads the effort so thin that none of them shows a result. Reels may be popular, but her own buyers told her they look elsewhere. YouTube being free doesn’t help if her customers don’t look for food sellers there.
quiz.learning_outcome: Choose one channel from where your interviews say customers are.

modules.title: Network and grow through people
modules.summary: Build a founder network from zero, ask for introductions well, use LinkedIn without spamming, and grow through referrals and partners.
modules.outcome: Map your founder network and write an introduction request, a LinkedIn note and a referral or partnership offer that people are glad to answer.

learn.title: Map your network from zero
learn.body:
You have a bigger network than you think. Draw it in four circles.
1. People you know: classmates, teachers, family, and the people you interviewed.
2. Your campus: the E-cell (entrepreneurship cell), the Institution’s Innovation Council if your college has one, and the college incubator. An incubator gives early founders mentors, space and sometimes small grants.
3. Your city and beyond: other incubators, alumni who started companies, startup meetups and competitions.
4. Online: LinkedIn and founder communities.

Worked example: Tenzin in Siliguri wants to sell organic tea by monthly subscription. His map had 40 names. They included an uncle with a tea-estate contact, an E-cell mentor and an alumnus who works at a D2C (direct-to-consumer) brand. A D2C brand sells online straight to its customers, not through shops. Next to each name he wrote what he could ask and what he could offer.

Common mistake: only chasing famous founders. People one step ahead of you are more likely to reply.

learn.title: Ask for introductions the right way
learn.body:
An introduction from someone both people trust works far better than a cold message. Use a double opt-in introduction. The connector first asks the other person whether they want to meet you, and only then introduces you.

Make it easy with a short “forwardable” message, written so the connector can forward it as it is. Say who you are, why this person, your specific ask, and how much time it needs.

Worked example: Tenzin wrote to his E-cell mentor:
“Could you ask Meera Das whether she’d take a 15-minute call? I run a small organic tea subscription in Siliguri with 25 paying customers. She grew a D2C tea brand’s repeat orders, and I want to ask how she reduced cancellations. Happy to work around her time.”

Afterwards, thank the connector and tell them what happened. Common mistake: a vague ask like “Can you connect me to someone in D2C?”

learn.title: LinkedIn done right, without spam
learn.body:
LinkedIn works when you are specific and few. First, finish your profile: a clear photo, a headline such as “Building an organic tea subscription | BBA student, Siliguri”, and two lines about what you are working on.

When you invite someone, add a short note: why them, one specific thing you noticed, and a small ask. When we checked LinkedIn’s Help Centre in October 2026, free members could add personal notes to only a few invitations a month. It also warned that many ignored or rapid invitations can restrict your account, and that automation tools are not allowed. So send a few good notes, never a mass of them.

Worked example: Tenzin pasted an alumnus’s public post into a free AI chatbot. He asked for three short notes mentioning that post. Then he checked each fact and cut the flattery. Never paste private messages or other people’s phone numbers into AI tools.

learn.title: Grow through referrals and partnerships
learn.body:
Your customers and neighbours can grow your business for you. A referral is when a happy customer brings a friend. Make it easy: ask right after a good moment, such as a delivery, and reward both people.

Worked example: Tenzin offered “₹50 off for you and ₹50 off for your friend”. That made each referred customer cost ₹100. Customers from his Instagram posts had cost about ₹180 each. Referrals were cheaper, and those friends trusted the product from the start.

A partnership is an agreement with another group that serves the same customers. Each side must gain something. Tenzin’s college canteen agreed to stock his tea packs and keep 15% of each sale. A campus hiking club put his tea in its trip kits in return for a discount.

Common mistake: a partnership with nothing written down. Write one paragraph: who does what, who earns what, and how either side can end it.

tasks.title: Map your founder network
tasks.prompt:
Draw your four circles on paper or in a notes app, for your own idea or for Tenzin’s tea subscription.
1. Put at least 20 people or places across the circles (use initials for people).
2. Next to each, write one thing you could ask and one thing you could offer.
3. Find out whether your college has an E-cell, an Innovation Council or an incubator, and how to contact it. Ask a teacher or a senior, or search your college website.
4. Circle the three contacts to approach first, and say why.
tasks.hint: What you can offer is often small but useful: feedback on their product, help at an event, a share of your customer insights, or simply a good question.

tasks.title: Write three messages people will answer
tasks.prompt:
Write three messages for your own idea:
1. A forwardable introduction request to a connector (under 80 words), with a specific ask and the time it needs.
2. A LinkedIn invitation note to an alumnus or founder that mentions something specific they shared publicly.
3. A referral offer for your customers, or a partnership offer to a club or shop. Say what each side gains.
Use a free AI chatbot for first drafts. Then remove any flattery, vague lines or facts you can’t check, and note what you changed.
tasks.hint: Read each message as the person receiving it. Can they say yes in one reply? Do they know exactly what you want and how long it takes?

reflection.prompt: Who has already helped you this year, even in a small way? How could you thank them, or give something back, before you ask for anything new?
reflection.hint: Strong networks are built on giving as well as asking. A short update on what their help led to is a good thank-you.

quiz.title: Asking for an introduction
quiz.scenario: Rhea in Bhopal runs baking classes with 30 paying students. She wants advice on running classes online. Her E-cell mentor knows Kavita Menon, who runs a large online cooking channel.
quiz.question: Which message to her mentor is best for him to forward?
options: “Could you ask Kavita if she’d take a 15-minute call? I teach baking in Bhopal to 30 paying students and want to ask how she moved online.”
“Could you connect me with someone who knows about online classes? Anyone at all would really help me, and I’m flexible about when we talk.”
“Please send Kavita my number and my full business plan. I would love her to invest in my classes, or to partner with me on her channel.”
“Hi! I’m Rhea, a huge fan of Kavita’s channel. Could you add the three of us to a WhatsApp group so that we can all chat about baking sometime?”
quiz.explanation: It can be forwarded as it is: who Rhea is, why Kavita, one specific question and how much time it needs. Kavita can say yes or no in one reply.
quiz.why_wrong: “Someone who knows about online classes” is too vague for the mentor to act on. Sending her number and plan and asking for investment is a big ask of a stranger, with no agreed time. A group chat connects them before Kavita has agreed, and “chat sometime” has no clear ask.
quiz.learning_outcome: Write introduction requests that are specific and forwardable.

quiz.title: An introduction from the incubator
quiz.scenario: Your college incubator’s manager offers to introduce you to an alumnus who runs a D2C skincare brand. You want to ask him how he found his first stockists.
quiz.question: What should you ask the manager to do, if you want a double opt-in introduction?
options: Ask the alumnus first, and connect you both only if he agrees to talk
Give you the alumnus’s phone number, so that you can call him yourself
Add the two of you to a WhatsApp group with a short introduction
Email the alumnus with you in copy, attaching your full pitch deck
quiz.explanation: In a double opt-in introduction, the connector checks with the other person before connecting you. The alumnus agrees first, so he is ready to help when you write, and the manager’s trust with him is protected.
quiz.why_wrong: Sharing his number without asking puts him on the spot and uses up the manager’s goodwill. A WhatsApp group and an email in copy both connect you before he has agreed, and a full pitch deck turns a small question into a large ask.
quiz.learning_outcome: Ask connectors for double opt-in introductions.

quiz.title: Two hundred invitations a day
quiz.scenario: Sanjay wants advice from founders who studied at his college. A friend suggests a browser tool that sends 200 LinkedIn invitations a day, each with the same message.
quiz.question: What is the better approach?
options: Use the tool, since sending more invitations means more founders will reply
Send all 200 invitations by hand without notes, so that no tool is involved
Use AI to change the name in each note, then send all 200 with the tool
Choose a few founders and write each one a short note about their own work
quiz.explanation: A few specific notes, each mentioning something the founder shared publicly, get more replies than a mass of identical ones. LinkedIn’s Help Centre also says automation tools are not allowed and that many ignored invitations can restrict an account.
quiz.why_wrong: The tool breaks LinkedIn’s rules, and identical messages get ignored, which can restrict his account. Sending 200 by hand without notes is still a mass of invitations to people with no reason to accept. Changing only the name is still a mass message, sent by a tool that isn’t allowed.
quiz.learning_outcome: Reach out to a few people with specific notes, never in bulk.

quiz.title: Referral or Instagram
quiz.scenario: Ishaan in Shillong sells a monthly snack box. Last month, ₹1,800 of Instagram posts brought him 12 new customers. Now he offers referrals: ₹40 off for the customer and ₹40 off for the friend they bring.
quiz.question: What does one new customer cost through each channel?
options: Referral ₹40 and Instagram ₹150
Referral ₹80 and Instagram ₹1,800
Referral ₹80 and Instagram ₹150
Referral ₹40 and Instagram ₹1,800
quiz.explanation: Each referral gives ₹40 to the customer and ₹40 to the friend, so one new customer costs ₹80. Instagram cost ₹1,800 ÷ 12 = ₹150 a customer. Referrals are cheaper, and the friends arrive already trusting the product.
quiz.why_wrong: ₹40 counts only the friend’s discount and forgets the ₹40 given to the customer who referred them. ₹1,800 is the whole month’s Instagram spend, not the cost of one customer: divide it by the 12 customers it brought.
quiz.learning_outcome: Work out the cost of one new customer for each channel.

modules.title: Price and manage money
modules.summary: Set a price from what customers value, check you earn on every sale, include payment fees, plan cash week by week, and know how first funding works.
modules.outcome: Set a price and show in a rupee table that each customer earns back more than they cost to win, with a one-month cash-flow plan.

learn.title: Price from value, not just from cost
learn.body:
Many first founders add a markup to their cost and call it the price. This is called cost-plus pricing. It ignores what the product is worth to the customer.

Think of two limits. The floor is your cost for each unit: below it, you lose money on every sale. The ceiling is what the customer would pay for the next best option. Your price sits between them, set by the value of the problem you solve.

Worked example: Divya in Jaipur runs mock interviews for students before placement season. Each one-hour session costs her about ₹150 in calls, materials and a reviewer’s time. A coaching institute charges ₹2,000 a session. Free YouTube videos give no personal feedback. In her interviews, three students had paid ₹1,500 for a CV review. She chose ₹499 a session, or ₹1,299 for three.

Common mistake: pricing very low “because students can’t pay”, without asking them.

learn.title: Unit economics: do you earn on each sale?
learn.body:
Unit economics means the money in and out for one unit: one sale or one customer.

Contribution margin is the price minus the costs that come with each unit, such as ingredients, packaging, delivery and payment fees. CAC (customer acquisition cost) is your marketing spend divided by the number of new customers it brought.

Worked example: a campus tiffin service.
Price per meal: ₹120.
Ingredients ₹55 + packaging ₹8 + delivery ₹15 = ₹78.
Contribution per meal: ₹120 − ₹78 = ₹42.
It spent ₹1,000 on posters and samples and won 20 customers, so CAC = ₹1,000 ÷ 20 = ₹50.
If a customer orders 8 meals a month, they bring 8 × ₹42 = ₹336. That is well above ₹50.
If they order only once, ₹42 is less than ₹50: a loss.

So repeat orders matter as much as price. AI can set up this table in Google Sheets, but check its sums by hand.

learn.title: Count payment fees, and date them
learn.body:
Payment fees come out of every sale, so they belong in your unit economics. They change, so check the provider’s own page and write the date in your sheet.

UPI (checked 26 October 2026): NPCI’s FAQ of 15 September 2026 sets a fee of 0.4%, capped at ₹300, on UPI payments to merchants above ₹2,000. Payments up to ₹2,000, and payments between people, stay free. Small sellers receiving up to ₹1 lakh a month by UPI QR pay nothing. Sellers can’t pass the fee on to customers. NPCI postponed the start until after Diwali. The start date is to be announced, so check npci.org.in.
Worked example: Imran’s ₹1,200 phone stands are under ₹2,000, so UPI adds no fee.

Payment gateways handle cards, wallets and payment links. Razorpay’s pricing page (October 2026) lists 2% of each payment plus 18% GST on that fee for its standard plan.
Worked example: on a ₹1,000 order, fee ₹20 + GST ₹3.60 = ₹23.60. You receive ₹976.40.

learn.title: Plan cash week by week
learn.body:
Profit and cash are different. You can make a profit on paper and still run out of cash, because you pay for stock before customers pay you. Many young businesses fail this way.

A cash-flow plan lists money in and money out, week by week, and the cash left at the end of each week.

Worked example: Sneha in Bhubaneswar starts a candle business with ₹10,000 of savings.
Week 1: buys wax and jars for ₹7,000, sells ₹1,500. Cash left: ₹4,500.
Week 2: marketing ₹1,000, sells ₹2,500. Cash left: ₹6,000.
Week 3: more stock ₹4,000, sells ₹3,000. Cash left: ₹5,000.
Week 4: sells ₹3,500. Cash left: ₹8,500.
Her lowest point is week 1, not the end of the month.

Runway is how many months your cash lasts if you keep losing money at today’s rate. Cash ÷ monthly loss = runway in months. Example: ₹6,000 left and losing ₹2,000 a month gives 3 months of runway.

learn.title: How first funding works
learn.body:
Most student businesses start with their own money, in this rough order.
1. Bootstrapping: your savings and your sales. Pre-orders count too.
2. Friends and family. Write down whether the money is a gift, a loan with a repayment date, or a share of the business.
3. Competitions, college grants and incubator programmes. Ask your E-cell or incubator. Schemes open and close, so check that one is open on its official page.
4. Bank loans. For example, banks lend to small businesses under the PM MUDRA Yojana. Check the current limits on its official site.
5. Angel investors and venture capital funds. They buy shares and expect fast growth. They are rare at the idea stage, and they look for evidence such as paying customers.

Worked example: an investor offers ₹5 lakh for 10% of your business. That values the business at ₹5 lakh ÷ 10% = ₹50 lakh, including the investor’s ₹5 lakh.

Common mistake: chasing investors before you have customers.

tasks.title: Check a business’s unit economics
tasks.prompt:
Sneha sells scented candles through Instagram messages for ₹349 each, paid by UPI. Each candle costs her ₹120 in wax, jar and fragrance, ₹25 in packaging, and about ₹60 for delivery within the city. Last month she spent ₹2,000 on a boosted post and free samples and won 16 new customers. On average, a customer buys 1.5 candles in three months.
In Google Sheets (free) or on paper, work out:
1. The contribution per candle.
2. Her CAC.
3. The contribution from one customer over three months.
Then decide whether she earns back what each customer costs, and suggest two changes that would improve the numbers.
tasks.hint: Total the costs that come with each candle first. Do UPI fees apply to a ₹349 payment? Check the dated card. Then compare one customer’s contribution with what it cost to win them.

tasks.title: Price your offer and plan one month’s cash
tasks.prompt:
For your own idea:
1. Write your price floor (cost per unit), your ceiling (the next best option’s price) and your price, with one line of reason.
2. In Google Sheets (free), make a four-week cash-flow plan: starting cash, money in (sales, pre-orders, family money), money out (stock, marketing, delivery, fees, tools) and cash left each week.
3. Mark your lowest week, and name one source of first money that suits your stage, with a reason.
Ask a free AI chatbot which costs you might have missed, then check each suggestion against your real plan.
tasks.hint: Be honest about when money arrives. A pre-order paid today is cash this week; a promise to pay next month is not. Write the date next to every fee you looked up.

reflection.prompt: Would you rather start with your own small savings, family money, or an investor’s money? What would each one cost you, apart from rupees?
reflection.hint: Think about control, pressure and relationships. Family money can strain a relationship; investor money means sharing ownership and decisions.

quiz.title: Pricing mock discussions
quiz.scenario: Kunal in Chandigarh runs one-hour mock group discussions for MBA entrance students. Each session costs him about ₹180 to run. A coaching centre charges ₹1,200 a session. In his interviews, four students had paid seniors ₹600 to ₹800 for one-off sessions.
quiz.question: Which price is best supported by these facts?
options: ₹220: his ₹180 cost plus a 20% markup
₹99: students can’t afford to pay more
₹699: near what students already pay
₹1,500: a high price looks premium
quiz.explanation: His floor is the ₹180 cost and his ceiling is the coaching centre’s ₹1,200. ₹699 sits between them, close to what students already pay seniors, so it matches the value they place on a session. He should still test it with real buyers.
quiz.why_wrong: Cost plus 20% ignores what the session is worth to the buyer and leaves most of that value unearned. ₹99 is a guess about what students can pay, and his interviews show they already pay far more. ₹1,500 is above the next best option, so buyers would choose the coaching centre.
quiz.learning_outcome: Price between cost and the next best option, guided by what customers value.

quiz.title: Breakfast boxes
quiz.scenario: Megha sells breakfast boxes to hostel students for ₹250 each. Each box costs her ₹90 in food, ₹20 in packaging and ₹30 in delivery. She spent ₹3,000 on posters and samples and won 20 customers. On average, a customer buys 2 boxes. Ignore payment fees here.
quiz.question: Does she earn back what each customer cost her to win?
options: Yes: each customer brings ₹220 of contribution against a CAC of ₹150
No: each box brings ₹110 of contribution, which is less than the ₹150 CAC
Yes: each customer brings ₹500 of sales against a CAC of only ₹150
No: her CAC is ₹3,000, more than any one customer will ever bring
quiz.explanation: Contribution per box is ₹250 − ₹140 = ₹110. A customer buys 2 boxes, so brings ₹220. CAC is ₹3,000 ÷ 20 = ₹150. ₹220 is more than ₹150, so each customer earns back their cost, with ₹70 to spare.
quiz.why_wrong: Comparing one box’s ₹110 with the CAC forgets the second order. ₹500 is sales, not contribution: it ignores the ₹140 of costs in each box. ₹3,000 is the whole marketing spend; CAC divides it by the 20 customers it won.
quiz.learning_outcome: Compare one customer’s total contribution with the cost of winning them.

quiz.title: Last year’s fee
quiz.scenario: Arnav is building his unit-economics table in Google Sheets. For the payment-gateway fee, he copied a percentage from a blog post written last year.
quiz.question: What should he do about the fee?
options: Leave fees out of the table, since they are too small to matter
Keep the blog’s figure, since gateway fees rarely change much
Check the gateway’s own pricing page today, and note the date
Ask an AI chatbot for the current fee, and use the figure it gives
quiz.explanation: Fees change, so the reliable figure is on the provider’s own page, checked now. Writing the date next to it shows when to check again. The fee then goes into the cost of every sale in his table.
quiz.why_wrong: Fees come out of every sale, so leaving them out makes each sale look better than it is. A blog figure from last year may be out of date, because fees do change. An AI chatbot can give an old or invented figure, so its answer still needs checking on the provider’s page.
quiz.learning_outcome: Take fees from the provider’s own page, dated, and include them in costs.

quiz.title: Cash in week two
quiz.scenario:
Nisha starts selling block-printed dupattas with ₹8,000 of savings. Her four-week plan:
Week 1: ₹9,000 out (stock), ₹2,000 in.
Week 2: ₹2,500 out, ₹1,000 in.
Week 3: ₹1,000 out, ₹6,000 in.
Week 4: ₹500 out, ₹7,000 in.
quiz.question: What does her plan show?
options: The month ends at ₹11,000, more than she started with, so it needs no change
Her lowest point is week 1, at ₹1,000, so she is safe if week 1 goes well
She loses money over the month, as ₹13,000 goes out against ₹8,000 saved
Her cash falls below zero in week 2, so she must plan for that week now
quiz.explanation: Week by week: ₹8,000 − ₹9,000 + ₹2,000 = ₹1,000 after week 1, then ₹1,000 − ₹2,500 + ₹1,000 = −₹500 after week 2. She needs ₹500 more by then, or must move a cost later, even though the month ends at ₹11,000.
quiz.why_wrong: The month-end total hides week 2, when she can’t pay her costs. Week 1 is not the lowest point: week 2 goes ₹500 below zero. The ₹13,000 going out should be set against ₹16,000 of sales as well as her savings; over the month she ends ahead.
quiz.learning_outcome: Plan cash week by week: a profitable month can still run out of cash.

modules.title: Build your team
modules.summary: Choose co-founders well, split equity with vesting, agree who decides what, and work fairly with freelancers and interns.
modules.outcome: Write a team plan for your idea: who owns each area, the equity split and vesting you have or would offer a co-founder, and a first brief for a freelancer or intern.

learn.title: Choosing a co-founder
learn.body:
A co-founder is a partner who builds the business with you and owns part of it. Look for three things.
1. Skills that complement yours. One person builds the product, the other sells it.
2. The same commitment: hours each week, and a plan for what happens after placement offers.
3. Shared values about money, risk and honesty.

Test the partnership before you commit. Work together on a small project for two weeks, such as running your MVP test.

Worked example: Arjun and Priya in Chennai want to build a revision app for Class 12 students. Arjun codes; Priya has already sold 40 pre-orders to parents. Before agreeing to be co-founders, they asked each other: “How many hours a week can you give? What if one of us takes a job offer? How will we settle a disagreement?”

Common mistake: choosing your closest friend without having these conversations.

learn.title: Equity and vesting, written down early
learn.body:
Equity is ownership of the business, counted in shares. Common advice, including from the startup accelerator Y Combinator, is to split it nearly equally between founders who commit fully. Then add vesting.

Vesting means you earn your shares over time. A common plan is four years with a one-year cliff. If you leave before the first year ends, you keep none. At one year, a quarter vests. The rest vests month by month.

Worked example: Arjun and Priya split 50:50 with that plan. If Priya leaves after 18 months, she has earned 18 of 48 months: 18 ÷ 48 = 37.5% of her shares. That is 37.5% × 50% = 18.75% of the business. The unearned shares stay with the business for whoever does the work.

Common mistake: a spoken deal with no vesting. Write it down and both sign it now. You can make it formal when you register the business.

learn.title: Roles, decisions and how you work
learn.body:
Most fights between founders are about who decides. Give each area one owner. The owner listens to others, then decides.

Worked example: Arjun and Priya wrote this down.
Arjun owns the product and technology.
Priya owns sales, marketing and money.
They decide together on hiring, fundraising and anything above ₹10,000.
If they disagree on a joint decision, each writes down their reasons, they sleep on it, and then they ask their mentor.

Culture is simply how you work together. Write down three habits, and act on them. For example: “We reply to customers within two hours.” “We write every decision in a shared Google Doc.” “We never post fake reviews.”

AI can help. Paste your rough notes into a free chatbot and ask for a one-page roles document. Then check that it says what you agreed, not what the AI assumed. Common mistake: “we both do everything”.

learn.title: Freelancers and interns, done fairly
learn.body:
You don’t need full-time staff to start. A freelancer is paid for a piece of work. An intern works with you to learn.

For a freelancer, write a brief: the goal, the exact deliverables, the deadline, the budget and examples you like. Pay per deliverable, often half at the start and half on delivery, by UPI. Agree that you receive the original files.

Worked example: Priya’s brief for a designer: “A logo and three Instagram post templates for a Class 12 revision app. Deadline: 10 days. Budget: ₹4,000, half now and half on delivery. Send the Canva or Figma files with the final versions.”

For an intern, write a brief too. Include the work, the hours, what they will learn, who will guide them and the pay, agreed before they start. Common mistake: vague “help with marketing” internships, where the intern learns little and you get little done.

tasks.title: Advise three would-be co-founders
tasks.prompt:
Three friends in Nagpur are starting a delivery service for home-made pickles. Rahul will work full-time after graduating next month and builds the website. Ayesha is in her final year, gives 15 hours a week, and has made all 30 sales so far. Varun had the idea, gives about 5 hours a week, and starts a job in three months. They want to split equity 33:33:33 with nothing written down.
Write them a short note (under 200 words):
1. Who should be a co-founder, and who might be better as an adviser or early helper, with reasons.
2. A suggested split and vesting plan.
3. Three questions they must answer together this week.
tasks.hint: Compare commitment and contribution, not who had the idea. Ask what happens to Varun’s shares when his job starts. Vesting is the tool that answers that fairly.

tasks.title: Write your team plan, a hiring brief and team habits
tasks.prompt:
For your own idea:
1. Write who owns each area of your business (product, sales, money). If you have, or want, a co-founder, write the split and vesting you would propose, in two lines. Working alone? Write the split and vesting you would offer a co-founder.
2. Write a one-page brief for a freelancer or an intern you might need in the next month: the goal, deliverables, deadline, pay and how it is paid, who reviews the work, and (for an intern) what they will learn.
3. Write three habits for how your team works.
Write your points as rough notes first, then ask a free AI chatbot to turn them into a clear brief. Check that it promises nothing you can’t pay for or deliver.
tasks.hint: For the split, use the same test as for the pickle founders: commitment and contribution, with vesting. A good brief lets a stranger start work without asking you a question. Read yours as if you were the freelancer: is anything unclear?

reflection.prompt: What are you bad at, or don’t enjoy, that your business still needs? Who could do it, and what would make it fair for them?
reflection.hint: Founders often hire people like themselves. The best early partners are often strong where you are weak.

quiz.title: Leaving after 30 months
quiz.scenario: Three founders in Ahmedabad agreed in writing that Kiran owns 40% of their company, vesting over four years with a one-year cliff. Kiran leaves after 30 months.
quiz.question: How much of the company has Kiran earned?
options: 40%, because her full share was agreed in writing
10%, because only the part at the one-year cliff has vested
25%, because 30 of the 48 months of her 40% have vested
0%, because she left before the four years were over
quiz.explanation: At the one-year cliff a quarter vests, and the rest vests month by month. At 30 months she has earned 30 ÷ 48 = 62.5% of her 40%, which is 25% of the company. The unearned 15% stays with the business.
quiz.why_wrong: 40% ignores vesting: the agreement says she earns her shares over time. 10% counts only the quarter that vests at the cliff and forgets the 18 months after it. 0% mixes up the four-year vesting period with the one-year cliff, which she passed long ago.
quiz.learning_outcome: Work out vested equity: months served ÷ 48 × the share, once past the cliff.

quiz.title: Who decides
quiz.scenario: Asif and Leena run a phone-accessories business in Kozhikode and own it 50:50. Every week they argue about decisions, from Instagram posts to buying ₹15,000 of stock. Nothing about roles is written down.
quiz.question: Which written rule would best end the weekly arguments?
options: Leena owns marketing, Asif owns stock and money, and they decide jointly above ₹10,000
They both work on everything, and they discuss each decision until both of them agree
Asif makes every decision, because he was the one who had the idea for the business
They take turns, with one of them making all of the decisions in alternate weeks
quiz.explanation: Most founder arguments are about who decides. Giving each area one owner, who listens and then decides, ends the small arguments, and a rule for big spending keeps both of them involved where it matters most.
quiz.why_wrong: “Both on everything” is the setup that causes the weekly arguments. Who had the idea says nothing about who should decide each area, and it leaves Leena with no say. Alternating weeks makes decisions depend on the calendar, and each can undo the other’s choices.
quiz.learning_outcome: Give each area of the business one owner, and agree how joint decisions are made.

quiz.title: Briefing a designer
quiz.scenario: Priyanka needs a logo for her tuition centre in Ranchi. She has ₹5,000 and wants it within two weeks.
quiz.question: Which brief is best to send a freelance designer?
options: “A cool, modern logo for my tuition centre, quite soon. I will pay well and I trust your creative ideas.”
“Logo for a Ranchi tuition centre, due in 14 days. ₹5,000 paid in full once our centre starts making a profit.”
“Logo for a Ranchi tuition centre, due in 14 days. ₹5,000 by UPI, half now and half on delivery, with source files.”
“Logo for a Ranchi tuition centre, due in 14 days. ₹5,000 paid in full today. Please send the final logo as a JPG.”
quiz.explanation: It gives the deliverable, the deadline, the budget and the payment plan, and asks for the original files so Priyanka can change the logo later. Half now and half on delivery is fair to both sides.
quiz.why_wrong: “Cool and modern” and “will pay well” give the designer nothing definite to work to or agree on. Paying only when the centre makes a profit pushes her business risk onto the designer. Paying everything today removes any check on delivery, and a JPG alone means she can’t edit the logo later.
quiz.learning_outcome: Brief a freelancer with deliverables, deadline, budget, payment terms and files.

quiz.title: Before saying yes
quiz.scenario: Gaurav, a commerce student in Kanpur, wants to start a used-furniture resale business. His classmate Saloni, who has sold things online before, wants to join him as a co-founder. They have never worked together.
quiz.question: What should they do before agreeing to be co-founders?
options: Run a two-week test together, and agree on hours, job offers and disagreements
Sign a 50:50 split straight away, so that both of them feel fully committed
Compare their marks and CVs, to decide which of them should be the main founder
Wait to talk about roles and equity until the business is earning some money
quiz.explanation: Working together on a small project, such as an MVP test, shows how they actually work as a team. Agreeing on weekly hours, what happens if one takes a job offer, and how to settle disagreements prevents the most common co-founder break-ups.
quiz.why_wrong: Signing 50:50 first locks in a deal before they know whether they work well together. Marks and CVs say little about commitment or how someone handles disagreement. Waiting until there is money makes the talk harder, because there is more to argue over.
quiz.learning_outcome: Test a co-founder partnership and talk through commitment before committing.

questions.title: Ten different answers
questions.scenario: Riya plans a study-planner service for “all college students in Delhi”. She has done 10 interviews. Each person described a different problem: exam stress, hostel noise, too many apps, slow Wi-Fi and more.
questions.question: What does this tell her to do next?
options: Choose a smaller customer group, and interview people from that group
Build features that solve all ten problems, so that everyone is covered
Ask an AI chatbot which of the ten problems is the most common one
Interview 50 more Delhi students, so that a pattern becomes clear
