questions.explanation: When people in a group describe the problem in completely different ways, the group is too broad. A smaller, specific group, such as first-year hostel students before semester exams, is likely to share one problem she can test.
questions.why_wrong: Ten features for ten problems is building before she knows which problem is real. A chatbot can’t tell her what real students experience; only real people from a sharper group can. More interviews from the same broad group will keep giving scattered answers.
questions.learning_outcome: Narrow the customer group when answers scatter.

questions.title: A big crore figure
questions.scenario: Faisal is planning a doubt-solving service for Class 12 students in Lucknow. A free AI chatbot told him the coaching market in India is worth thousands of crores, but gave no source he could open. His mentor asks him for a market estimate.
questions.question: What should he give his mentor?
options: The chatbot’s figure, with a clear note that it came from an AI tool
The chatbot’s figure, as long as a second chatbot gives a similar one
A bottom-up estimate from numbers he can check, with guesses marked
No estimate, since market size can’t be known before he launches
questions.explanation: An AI figure is usable only if he can open its source and check it. Counting the students he can reach, then multiplying by a marked guess of the share who would pay and by the price, gives an estimate he can defend and test.
questions.why_wrong: Saying a number came from AI doesn’t make it true. Two chatbots can repeat the same invented or out-of-date figure. A bottom-up estimate is possible before launch: it simply marks which numbers are guesses still to test.
questions.learning_outcome: Use only AI figures you can source; build estimates bottom-up.

questions.title: The problem is real
questions.scenario: Kavya interviewed 8 working parents in Kochi about weekday dinners. Seven already pay a neighbour or a tiffin service ₹3,000 to ₹4,000 a month. She plans a weekly dinner subscription at ₹3,500 a month, paid in advance. Nobody has paid her anything yet.
questions.question: What is her best next step?
options: Offer a one-week trial on WhatsApp, and ask for payment in advance by UPI
Build a subscription app, since the interviews show the problem is real
Interview 20 more parents about how they manage weekday dinners now
Spend ₹5,000 on Instagram ads to see how many parents click on her page
questions.explanation: Her interviews already show the problem is real: parents spend money on it now. What she doesn’t know is whether they will pay her in advance, her riskiest assumption. A WhatsApp trial with a UPI advance tests exactly that, with free tools.
questions.why_wrong: An app takes weeks and still doesn’t test whether parents will pay her. More interviews about past behaviour repeat what she already knows. Ad clicks measure curiosity, not payment, and spend money before anyone has paid.
questions.learning_outcome: Move from evidence of a problem to an MVP that tests payment.

questions.title: Fourteen yeses
questions.scenario: Before his test, Aman wrote: “At least 5 of 20 hostel students pay a ₹100 advance for laundry pickup within 3 days.” After 3 days, 14 students said they would definitely use it, and 3 paid the advance.
questions.question: How should Aman report the result to his mentor?
options: A success: 14 of 20 (70%) want the service, far above his goal of 5
Goal missed: 3 paid, not 5, so he should ask why the others didn’t pay
Goal met, if he moves it to 3 of 20, since his first goal was too strict
A failure: only 3 of 20 paid, so he should drop the laundry idea now
questions.explanation: His goal was about paying, and he wrote it before the test: 3 is fewer than 5. The 14 “definitely” answers are promises, the bottom rung. Three real payments still matter, so asking the students who said yes but didn’t pay what stopped them shows what to change before he tests again.
questions.why_wrong: Counting promises as the result swaps the measure after the test. Moving the goal to 3 makes any result a success, which is exactly what writing it first prevents. Dropping the idea ignores three real payments and a gap he can investigate.
questions.learning_outcome: Report a test honestly against its goal; promises are not payments.

questions.title: The maybe
questions.scenario: Two days ago, a customer told Zoya “maybe next week” about her ₹999 skincare kit. Zoya sent one follow-up message yesterday. There is no reply yet.
questions.question: What should Zoya do now?
options: Message her every day until she gives a clear yes or no
Add her to a broadcast list to see every new product
Send one short message with a clear next step, then stop
Ask a mutual friend to remind her that she said maybe
questions.explanation: One or two short follow-ups are polite and useful; after that, silence is an answer. A clear next step, such as “Shall I keep one for you for Saturday?”, makes it easy to reply.
questions.why_wrong: Daily messages feel like pressure and can lose her as a future customer. A broadcast list sends her messages she didn’t ask for. Asking a friend to remind her adds social pressure, which can harm trust and the friendship.
questions.learning_outcome: Follow up once or twice with a clear next step, then stop.

questions.title: The screenshot
questions.scenario: A buyer sends Mohit a screenshot of a ₹600 UPI payment for two T-shirts. Mohit labels his WhatsApp Business chats “New”, “Paid” and “Delivered”.
questions.question: When should he label this chat “Paid”?
options: As soon as the screenshot arrives, since it shows the payment
When the ₹600 shows as received in his own bank or UPI app
When the buyer sends a message confirming that they have paid
After delivery, when the buyer says the T-shirts have arrived
questions.explanation: A screenshot can be faked, or can show a payment that later failed. The only proof is the money in his own account, so he checks his bank or UPI app before he labels the chat and sends the order.
questions.why_wrong: A screenshot is easy to fake or edit. A message saying “I’ve paid” is not money received. Waiting until delivery mixes two steps: he should confirm the payment before he sends the order, not after.
questions.learning_outcome: Count a sale as paid only when the money reaches your account.

questions.title: Two channels, one margin
questions.scenario: Tanvi sells homemade granola in Mumbai. Each order brings her ₹60 of contribution, and a customer orders about twice. In her ₹1,000 test, ₹600 of samples at a yoga studio won 6 customers, and a ₹400 boosted post won 2 customers.
questions.question: What should she do with her next marketing budget?
options: Put it into the boosted post, since a post reaches many more people
Split it between both channels again, since each one won customers
Stop spending, since one ₹60 order earns back neither ₹100 nor ₹200
Put it into the studio, where a customer costs ₹100 and brings ₹120
questions.explanation: Studio CAC is ₹600 ÷ 6 = ₹100 and post CAC is ₹400 ÷ 2 = ₹200. A customer brings about 2 × ₹60 = ₹120, so studio customers earn back their cost and post customers lose ₹80 each. One small test is a hint, so she should keep measuring.
questions.why_wrong: Reach doesn’t help if the post’s customers cost ₹200 and bring ₹120. Splitting again ignores what the test showed. Comparing one ₹60 order with the CAC forgets that customers order about twice.
questions.learning_outcome: Compare each channel’s CAC with what a customer brings.

questions.title: For everyone who loves food
questions.scenario: Kiran in Chennai sells ready-to-cook dosa batter. Her positioning is “for everyone who loves good food”, and she posts a little on four platforms. After a month she has 2 orders. Her interviews showed that couples who both work need quick breakfasts, and hear about home sellers through apartment WhatsApp groups.
questions.question: What is the best advice for her?
options: Add two more platforms, so that her posts reach more people each week
Boost every post she has made, so that more people see each of them
Offer 50% off for a month, so that more people are tempted to try it
Aim at working couples, through their apartments’ WhatsApp groups
questions.explanation: Her interviews already name the customer and the problem, and show where those customers look for sellers. Narrow positioning and one channel they use, with each group admin’s permission, give her effort a chance to show a result.
questions.why_wrong: More platforms spread the same thin effort further. Boosting posts with no clear customer pays to reach people who may not want batter. A big discount attracts bargain-hunters and hides whether her real customers value the product.
questions.learning_outcome: Use interview evidence to set positioning and pick one channel.

questions.title: Ten lakh from investors
questions.scenario: Rahul, a second-year student in Hyderabad, has an idea for a campus delivery app. He has no customers yet. He plans to message 100 angel investors on LinkedIn, asking for ₹10 lakh.
questions.question: What is the best advice for Rahul?
options: Send all 100 messages, since just one investor saying yes would be enough
Win first paying users with a small MVP, and ask the E-cell for advice
Ask his family for the ₹10 lakh instead, with nothing written down
Take a ₹10 lakh bank loan, so that he gives away none of his shares
questions.explanation: Investors are rare at the idea stage, and they look for evidence such as paying customers. A small MVP gets that evidence cheaply, and his E-cell or incubator can advise him and later make warm, double opt-in introductions.
questions.why_wrong: A hundred identical messages to strangers are spam, and with no customers there is little for an investor to back. Family money with nothing written down risks the relationship: write whether it is a gift, a loan or a share. A big loan for an untested idea leaves him owing money whether or not it works.
questions.learning_outcome: Get evidence before chasing investors, and use your network well.

questions.title: The canteen deal
questions.scenario: Divya’s college canteen in Jaipur has agreed to stock her millet energy bars and keep a share of each sale. They shook hands on it yesterday.
questions.question: What should Divya do next?
options: Rely on the handshake, since a written note could look like mistrust
Write one paragraph on who does what, who earns what and how to end it
Get a long contract from an AI chatbot and ask the canteen to sign it
Write down the share of each sale that the canteen keeps, and nothing else
questions.explanation: A short written note covers what partners usually fall out over: who does what (stocking, display, restocking), who earns what, and how either side can end the deal. It protects the relationship as well as the money.
questions.why_wrong: A handshake leaves each side remembering different terms. A long AI-written contract that neither side has read may contain terms nobody intended, and can put a small partner off. Writing only the share leaves out who restocks, what happens to unsold bars and how to end the deal.
questions.learning_outcome: Write partnership terms down in one short paragraph.

questions.title: Phone stands
questions.scenario: Ravi sells personalised phone stands for ₹400 through a payment link. Each stand costs ₹220 in materials, packing and delivery. Today he checked the gateway’s own pricing page, which lists a total fee of 2.36% of each payment. His CAC is ₹150, and each customer buys one stand.
questions.question: How much does each customer leave him after the CAC?
questions.explanation: The fee is 2.36% of ₹400 = ₹9.44, so contribution is ₹400 − ₹220 − ₹9.44 = ₹170.56. Taking away the ₹150 CAC leaves ₹20.56 from each customer.
questions.why_wrong: ₹30.00 leaves out the payment fee, which comes out of every sale. ₹170.56 is the contribution per stand, before the cost of winning the customer. ₹25.75 works out the fee on the ₹180 margin instead of on the full ₹400 payment.
questions.learning_outcome: Include a dated payment fee in contribution, then compare with CAC.

questions.title: Leaving before the cliff
questions.scenario: Neel, Farah and Joseph signed a split of 30%, 35% and 35%, each vesting over four years with a one-year cliff. Neel leaves after 11 months to take a job.
questions.question: How much of the company does Neel keep?
options: 0%: his 30% stays with the business, for those who do the work
7.5%: a quarter of his 30%, and the rest stays with the business
About 6.9%: 11 of 48 months, and the rest stays with the business
30%: shares that were signed for can’t be taken back from a founder
questions.explanation: With a one-year cliff, nothing vests until the first year is complete. Neel left at 11 months, so he keeps none, and his unvested shares stay with the business for the founders who stay and do the work.
questions.why_wrong: 7.5% treats him as if he had reached the cliff, but he left a month before it. 6.9% counts month by month from the start, ignoring the cliff. 30% ignores the vesting they signed: the agreement itself says shares are earned over time.
questions.learning_outcome: Apply the cliff: leaving before it means no shares vest.

questions.title: A six-week intern
questions.scenario: Your E-cell offers you a first-year student as an intern for six weeks, to help with your snack-box business’s Instagram page.
questions.question: Which plan is fairest and most useful?
options: “Help with marketing and anything else that comes up. Flexible hours; let’s see how it goes.”
“Plan and post 3 Reels a week, 8 hours a week. You learn content testing; I review weekly. Pay agreed now.”
“Plan and post 3 Reels a week, full-time, to show commitment. Pay will be a small share of the company later.”
“Run the whole Instagram page on your own for six weeks. You get a certificate at the end if the page grows.”
questions.explanation: It names the work, the hours, what the intern will learn, who guides them, and pay agreed before they start. The intern learns something real, and the business gets a clear piece of work done.
questions.why_wrong: “Help with marketing and anything else” is the vague internship where the intern learns little and little gets done. Full-time hours for an unclear future share asks a lot and promises nothing definite. Running the page alone, for a certificate only if it grows, gives no guidance and no fair pay.
questions.learning_outcome: Brief an intern with the work, hours, learning, guidance and pay.

questions.title: The one-page plan
questions.scenario: A mentor reviews Sana’s plan for a weekly snack box in Pune. She has 7 interviews, 3 introductions and 2 paid advances. Her price is ₹199, and each box costs ₹170 to make and deliver. Her ₹1,000 test on her one channel, college WhatsApp groups, won 8 customers. Most customers buy only once. She plans to spend ₹10,000 on marketing next month.
questions.question: What is the most serious problem in her plan?
options: Seven interviews are too few to show that the problem is real for her customers
She markets on only one channel, so she misses the customers on other platforms
Each customer brings ₹29 but costs ₹125 to win, so more marketing deepens the loss
Her plan names no investor, so she has no way to pay for ₹10,000 of marketing
questions.explanation: Contribution is ₹199 − ₹170 = ₹29 a box, and CAC is ₹1,000 ÷ 8 = ₹125. With one purchase each, every new customer loses her about ₹96, so ₹10,000 more marketing would lose money faster. She needs a higher price, lower costs or repeat orders before she spends more.
questions.why_wrong: Seven interviews with introductions and paid advances already reach the top rungs of the ladder, which is enough at this stage. Starting with one channel is right, not a weakness. Investor money would only pay for the losses; the unit economics must work first.
questions.learning_outcome: Read a whole plan and find the problem that matters most: losing money on every customer.

questions.title: AI and interview notes
questions.scenario: Rohan has notes from 6 customer interviews, including names and phone numbers. He wants a free AI chatbot to group the notes into patterns for his mentor.
questions.question: Which way of using the chatbot is sound?
options: Paste in the full notes so the chatbot has every detail, and send its summary on
Remove names and numbers, ask for themes, and check each theme against his notes
Remove names and numbers, and ask it to add 20 realistic interviews for a bigger sample
Remove names and numbers, ask for themes, and send them on as they are, since it read all six
questions.explanation: Removing personal details protects the people who spoke to him. Grouping notes is a good job for AI, but chatbots can overstate or invent a pattern, so each theme must be checked against what people actually said before it goes to his mentor.
questions.why_wrong: Pasting names and phone numbers shares people’s personal details without need. AI-made interviews are synthetic users, not evidence, and they would hide the real pattern. Sending the themes unchecked trusts the AI, when it can report a pattern that nobody mentioned.
questions.learning_outcome: Protect interviewees’ details and check every AI summary against the source.

project.brief: Over about two weeks, with your mentor’s guidance, take one real business idea (your own, or one from your campus) from a guess to evidence. Talk to at least 5 real people from your customer group, and win at least one commitment: a next meeting, an introduction, a trial booked or a payment. Then write a one-page plan that a mentor or an early supporter could act on. Your mentor helps you choose the idea and the customer group, and reviews your interview script before you start. Plan for about 8 hours of work spread over the two weeks: conversations take time to arrange, so start them in the first week.
deliverables: A problem statement for one named customer group, with a bottom-up market estimate whose numbers each have a source you checked

An interview log of at least 5 real conversations (names removed, with permission), each with the date, the person’s role and what they had already done about the problem, plus a summary of the patterns

Proof of at least one commitment (such as a UPI payment screenshot with personal details hidden, a booked trial, or an introduction), with a note on which rung of the evidence ladder each piece of evidence reaches
Your MVP and the result of testing it with 5 users, set against the success goal you wrote before the test

A one-page plan: the customer, the offer and price, unit economics and a one-month cash flow in rupees, the first marketing channel, who owns which area (if you have co-founders, the equity split and vesting you have agreed in writing; a solo founder writes the split and vesting they would offer a co-founder), and the next 30 days
A note to your mentor on what the evidence changed in your idea, and where you used AI and how you checked it

rubric.name: Evidence quality
rubric.description: At least 5 real conversations about past behaviour, each placed on the right rung of the evidence ladder, and at least one real commitment shown

rubric.name: Problem and customer
rubric.description: One named customer group and its problem in their own words, with a bottom-up estimate whose sources are checked and guesses marked

rubric.name: MVP test
rubric.description: The riskiest assumption is named, the success goal was written before the test, and the result is reported honestly against it

rubric.name: Price and money
rubric.description: A price set between cost and the next best option, with contribution, CAC, dated fees and a one-month cash flow that add up

rubric.name: Plan and judgement
rubric.description: The next 30 days and the channel follow from the evidence, each area has one owner, the equity split and vesting are written (agreed, or proposed if solo), and every use of AI is named and checked
